item.title: World shares rise after technology shares advance on Wall Street ahead of U.S. inflation data
item.description: Global markets were higher Tuesday after U.S. stocks rallied, recovering most of their big losses from last week, while investors awaited U.S. inflation data for October.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — The U.S. stock market dipped Tuesday after a report showed inflation was worse across the country last month than economists expected. The S&P 500 slipped 0.4 per cent and gave back some of its big rally from the day before. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 157 points, or 0.3 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 0.7 per cent. Pressure from the bond market undercut stocks following the discouraging report on inflation. People had to pay prices for groceries, electricity and other costs of living that were higher last month than economists expected. That could push the Federal Reserve to hike its main interest rate at its next meeting in December and beyond. Higher interest rates can help rein in inflation, but they do so by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money and by slowing the overall economy. Higher rates also make investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks and other investments. One Fed official even hinted the central bank may increase the federal funds rate by double the typical amount next month because of how high inflation has remained for years. Speaking in London before the inflation report was released, Fed Gov. Christopher Waller said “a stronger policy move may be needed” if the report showed an important underlying measure of inflation rose by 0.3 per cent from September. In that case, he said the Fed should consider hiking the federal funds rate by half a percentage point rather than the typical quarter point. Moving by only the usual amount could “put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.” Shortly afterward, Tuesday’s inflation report showed that the underlying measure of inflation Waller was worried about was exactly 0.3 per cent, the threshold he had set. It’s the Fed’s job to keep inflation under control, along with keeping the job market strong. That sent yields jumping in the bond market as traders upped their forecasts for coming hikes to rates by the Fed. The yield on the 10-year Treasury leaped to 4.99 per cent from 4.88 per cent late Monday. It’s a notable move for the bond market, and the yield helps set where rates are for mortgages and other loans going to U.S. households and businesses. The 10-year Treasury yield had been dropping since early October, when it topped 5.30 per cent as worries spiked about high inflation, higher interest rates, the U.S. government’s big debt and other concerns. Tuesday’s jump in yields came even though oil prices fell again. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell 1.2 per cent to US$91.49. President Donald Trump said late Monday that the war in Iran, which sent oil prices much higher, “militarily is effectively over.” Brent’s price has been falling from more than US$112 at the start of the month amid uncertainty about what will happen with the war with Iran. Jumps in Treasury yields push downward on prices for all kinds of stocks, and they can particularly hurt companies in the real-estate business. Higher mortgage rates can keep potential customers away from homebuilders, for example, and Lennar fell 5.4 per cent for one of the sharper losses in the S&P 500. Rival homebuilders also fell, including drops of 3.8 per cent for D.R. Horton and 3.9 per cent for PulteGroup. Builders FirstSource, which sells crown mouldings, cabinets and other products to homebuilders, sank 4.6 per cent. The single heaviest weight on the S&P 500 was Nvidia, which fell 5.5 per cent. It’s been under pressure since its board announced an investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, who admitted to a relationship with a woman who, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for China. It’s also been swinging amid broader worries that have knocked the artificial-intelligence industry around recently. Democratic victories in statehouses across the country last week raised concerns about possible restrictions on construction of AI data centres. That built on top of longstanding worries that AI stock prices had shot too high and were in a bubble. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, dropped 3.9 per cent. Micron Technology, which sells memory for computers, fell 1.1 per cent. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, slipped 0.5 per cent. Other AI-related stocks held up better, though. Broadcom climbed 3.9 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices rose 1.3 per cent. The recent shakiness for AI-related stocks had raised questions about whether Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, may delay its initial public offering of stock. But Anthropic said in a filing with U.S. regulators on Tuesday that it’s looking to sell its stock at a price valuing the company at roughly US$1.3 trillion. That would make it one of the most valuable companies on Wall Street, worth more than Walmart, JPMorgan Chase, ExxonMobil or Coca-Cola. All told, the S&P 500 fell 29.01 points to 7,520.93. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 157.86 to 52,231.89, and the Nasdaq composite sank 187.26 to 25,065.87. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 4.4 per cent for one of the world’s biggest gains on strength for its two tech giants that have benefited from the AI boom, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Writers Elaine Lai and Matt Ott contributed to this report

item.title: Further interest rate hikes might be needed: Bank of Canada
item.description: The Bank of Canada’s governing council thinks it might need to raise interest rates further, but it’s proceeding carefully, according to a summary of deliberations.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — The Bank of Canada’s governing council thinks it might need to raise interest rates further, but it’s proceeding carefully, according to a summary of deliberations of its recent decision to raise its key policy rate for the first time since 2023. According to the report, the council acknowledged it faced considerable uncertainty and said it would take its monetary policy decisions one meeting at a time. The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month to reduce the risk that stubbornly high oil prices become persistent inflation. The summary says the council members agreed that monetary policy cannot lower global energy prices, but can prevent them from leading to generalized inflation. The decision came as the Bank of Canada raised its outlook for the annual inflation rate to hit 3.5 per cent at the end of this year and remain above three per cent for much of 2027. The summary of deliberations said higher costs largely haven’t been passed through to consumers so far, but the bank’s surveys suggest businesses expect to raise some prices over the next year. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.
